The United States of America (USA), also known as the United States (U.S.) or America, is a country primarily located in North America. It is a federal republic consisting of 50 states and a federal capital district, Washington, D.C. The 48 contiguous states border Canada to the north and Mexico to the south, with the semi-exclave of Alaska in the northwest and the archipelago of Hawaii in the Pacific Ocean. The United States also asserts sovereignty over five major island territories and various uninhabited islands in Oceania and the Caribbean.[k] It is a megadiverse country, with the world's fourth-largest total area[l] and third-largest population, exceeding 341 million.[m]

Paleo-Indians migrated from North Asia to North America at least 15,000 years ago and formed various civilizations. Beginning in 1607, British colonization established the Thirteen Colonies. The 18th-century American Enlightenment spread values of republicanism and liberalism there, and clashes with the British Crown over taxation without parliamentary representation, among other denied rights, sparked the American Revolution. Independence from Great Britain was formally declared in the Lee Resolution of July 2, 1776, two days before the Declaration of Independence. Victory in the 1775–1783 Revolutionary War brought international recognition of U.S. sovereignty.

The U.S. expanded westward through the purchase, settlement, and conquest of European- and Indigenous-controlled territory. As more states joined the Union, a sectional division over slavery led 11 Southern states to declare secession and form the Confederate States of America, fighting the Union in the Civil War of 1861–1865. With the United States' victory and reunification, slavery was abolished. By 1900, the U.S. emerged as a great power, a status solidified after its involvement in World War I. Following Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, it entered World War II on the Allied side. The war's aftermath left the U.S. and the Soviet Union as rival superpowers, vying for geopolitical dominance during the Cold War. The Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 left the U.S. as the world's sole superpower, although it has faced competition from China in the 2020s.

The U.S. federal government is a republic under the Constitution, which created a separation of powers among legislative, executive, and judicial branches. Executive authority is vested in a president, while Congress is a bicameral national legislature composed of the House of Representatives (a lower house based on population) and the Senate (an upper house based on equal representation for each state). The Supreme Court exercises judicial review, under which it may hold laws or governmental actions unconstitutional. Federalism grants substantial autonomy to the 50 states.

A developed country, the United States ranks high in economic competitiveness, innovation, and higher education. Its economy accounts for over a quarter of nominal global GDP and has been the world's largest since about 1890. The U.S. is the wealthiest country, with the highest disposable household income per capita among OECD members, though its wealth inequality is highly pronounced. American culture, shaped by centuries of immigration, is diverse and globally influential. The U.S. makes up nearly a third of global military spending and is widely considered to have the most powerful armed forces in the world. A member of numerous international organizations, it plays a dominant role in global political, cultural, economic, and military affairs.

Etymology
Further information: Names of the United States, Demonyms for the United States, United Colonies, and Naming of the Americas

Documented use of the phrase "United States of America" dates back to January 2, 1776. On that day, Stephen Moylan, a Continental Army aide to General George Washington, wrote a letter to Joseph Reed, Washington's aide-de-camp, seeking to go "with full and ample powers from the United States of America to Spain" to seek assistance in the Revolutionary War effort.[28][29] The first known public usage is an anonymous essay published in the Williamsburg newspaper The Virginia Gazette on April 6, 1776.[28] Sometime on or after June 11, 1776, Thomas Jefferson wrote "United States of America" in a rough draft of the Declaration of Independence,[28] which was adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.[30]

The term "United States" and its initialism "U.S.", used as nouns or as adjectives in English, are common short names for the country. The initialism "USA", a noun, is also common.[31] "United States" and "U.S." are the established terms throughout the U.S. federal government, with prescribed rules.[n] "The States" is an established colloquial shortening of the name, used particularly from abroad;[33] "stateside" is the corresponding adjective or adverb.[34]

"America" is the feminine form of the first name of Americus Vesputius, the Latinized name of Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512);[o] it was first used as a place name by the German cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann in 1507.[35][p] Vespucci proposed that the West Indies discovered by Christopher Columbus in 1492 were part of a previously unknown landmass and not among the Indies at the eastern limit of Asia.[36][37][38] In English, the term "America" (used without a qualifier) seldom refers to topics unrelated to the United States. "The Americas" is the general term to describe the totality of the continents of North and South America.[39]

History
Main article: History of the United States
For a topical guide, see Outline of the history of the United States.
Indigenous peoples
Main articles: History of Native Americans in the United States and Pre-Columbian era
Cliff Palace, a settlement of ancestors of the Native American Pueblo peoples in present-day Montezuma County, Colorado, built between c. 1200 and 1275[40]

The first inhabitants of North America migrated from Siberia at least 15,000 years ago, either across the Bering land bridge or along the now-submerged Ice Age coastline.[41][42] The Clovis culture, which appeared around 11,000 BCE in North America, is believed to be the first widespread culture in the Americas.[43][44] Over time, Indigenous North American cultures grew increasingly sophisticated, and some, such as the Mississippian culture, developed agriculture, architecture, and complex societies.[45] In the post-archaic period, the Mississippian cultures were located in the midwestern, eastern, and southern regions, and the Algonquian in the Great Lakes region and along the Eastern Seaboard, while the Hohokam culture and Ancestral Puebloans inhabited the Southwest.[46] Native population estimates of what is now the United States before the arrival of European colonizers range from around 500,000[47][48] to nearly 10 million.[48][49] In 2024, an estimated 3.43 million people in the United States identified as American Indian or Alaska Native alone (thus, identifying with no other racial category) and represented approximately 1% of the U.S. population.[50] An additional 5.68 million people identified as American Indian or Alaska Native in combination with one or more other races, bringing the total of those identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native to approximately 9.11 million.[51]

European exploration, colonization and conflict (1513–1765)
Main articles: Colonial history of the United States and Colonial American military history
The colonial possessions of Britain (the Thirteen Colonies in pink and others in purple), France (in blue), and Spain (in orange) in North America, 1750

Christopher Columbus began exploring the Caribbean for Spain in 1492, leading to Spanish-speaking settlements and missions from what are now Puerto Rico and Florida to New Mexico and California. The first Spanish colony in the present-day continental United States was Spanish Florida, chartered in 1513.[52][53][54][55] After several settlements failed there due to starvation and disease, Spain's first permanent town, Saint Augustine, was founded in 1565.[56]

France established its own settlements in French Florida in 1562, but they were either abandoned (Charlesfort, 1563)[57] or destroyed by Spanish raids (Fort Caroline, 1565). Permanent French settlements were founded much later along the Great Lakes (Fort Detroit, 1701), the Mississippi River (St. Louis, 1764) and especially the Gulf of Mexico (New Orleans, 1718).[58] Early European colonies also included the thriving Dutch colony of New Nederland (settled 1626, present-day New York) and the small Swedish colony of New Sweden (settled 1638 in what became Delaware). British colonization of the East Coast began with the Virginia Colony (1607) and the Plymouth Colony (Massachusetts, 1620).[59][60]

The Mayflower Compact in Massachusetts and the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut established precedents for local representative self-governance and constitutionalism that would develop throughout the American colonies.[61][62] While European settlers in what is now the United States experienced conflicts with Native Americans, they also engaged in trade, exchanging European tools for food and animal pelts.[63][q] Relations ranged from close cooperation to warfare and massacres. The colonial authorities often pursued policies that forced Native Americans to adopt European lifestyles, including conversion to Christianity.[67][68] Along the eastern seaboard, settlers trafficked Africans through the Atlantic slave trade, largely to provide manual labor on plantations.[69]

The original Thirteen Colonies[r] that would later found the United States were administered as possessions of the British Empire by Crown-appointed governors,[70] though local governments held elections open to most white male property owners.[71][72] The colonial population grew rapidly from Maine to Georgia, eclipsing Native American populations;[73] by the 1770s, the natural increase of the population was such that only a small minority of Americans had been born overseas.[74] The colonies' distance from Britain facilitated the entrenchment of self-governance,[75] and the First Great Awakening, a series of Christian revivals, fueled colonial interest in guaranteed religious liberty.[76]

American Revolution and the early republic (1765–1800)
Main articles: History of the United States (1776–1789), History of the United States (1789–1815), American Revolution, and Founding Fathers of the United States
The Declaration of Independence portrait depicts the Committee of Five presenting the Declaration to the Continental Congress on June 28, 1776, in Philadelphia.

Following its victory in the French and Indian War, Britain began to assert greater control over local affairs in the Thirteen Colonies, resulting in growing political resistance. One of the primary grievances of the colonists was the denial of their rights as Englishmen, particularly the right to representation in the British government that taxed them. To demonstrate their dissatisfaction and resolve, the First Continental Congress met in 1774 and passed the Continental Association, a colonial boycott of British goods enforced by local "committees of safety" that proved effective. The British attempt to then disarm the colonists resulted in the 1775 Battles of Lexington and Concord, igniting the American Revolutionary War. At the Second Continental Congress, the colonies appointed George Washington Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army, and created a committee that named Thomas Jefferson to draft the Declaration of Independence. Two days after the Second Continental Congress passed the Lee Resolution to create an independent, sovereign nation, the Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776.[77] The political values of the American Revolution evolved from an armed rebellion demanding reform within an empire to a revolution that created a new social and governing system founded on the defense of liberty and the protection of inalienable natural rights; equality under the law; sovereignty of the people;[78] republicanism over monarchy, aristocracy, and other hereditary political power; civic virtue; and an intolerance of political corruption.[79] The Founding Fathers of the United States, who included Washington, Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, John Jay, James Madison, Thomas Paine, and many others, were inspired by Classical, Renaissance, and Enlightenment philosophies and ideas.[80][81]

Though in practical effect since its drafting in 1777, the Articles of Confederation were ratified in 1781 and formally established a decentralized government that operated until 1789.[77] After the British surrender at the siege of Yorktown in 1781, American sovereignty was internationally recognized by the Treaty of Paris (1783), through which the U.S. also gained territory stretching west to the Mississippi River, north to present-day Canada, and south to Spanish Florida.[82] The Northwest Ordinance (1787) established the precedent by which the country's territory would expand with the admission of new states, rather than the expansion of existing states.[83]

The U.S. Constitution was drafted at the 1787 Constitutional Convention to overcome certain limitations of the Articles. It went into effect in 1789, creating a federal republic governed by three separate branches that together formed a system of checks and balances.[84] George Washington was elected the country's first president under the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights (a series of ten amendments to the Constitution) was adopted in 1791 to allay skeptics' concerns about the power of the more centralized government.[85] Washington's resignation as Commander-in-Chief after the Revolutionary War and his later refusal to run for a third term as the country's first president established a precedent for the supremacy of civil authority in the United States and the peaceful transfer of power.[86]

Westward expansion and Civil War (1800–1865)
Main articles: History of the United States (1815–1849) and History of the United States (1849–1865)
Territorial expansion of the United States

In the late 18th century, American settlers began to expand westward in larger numbers, many with a sense of manifest destiny.[87][88] The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 from France nearly doubled the territory of the United States.[89][90] Lingering issues with Britain remained, leading to the War of 1812, which was fought to a draw.[91] Spain ceded Florida and its Gulf Coast territory in 1819.[92]

The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, attempted to balance the desire of northern states to prevent the expansion of slavery into new territories with that of southern states to extend it there. Primarily, the compromise prohibited slavery in all other lands of the Louisiana Purchase north of the 36°30′ parallel.[93]

As Americans expanded further into territory inhabited by Native Americans, the federal government implemented policies of Indian removal or assimilation.[94][95] The most significant such legislation was the Indian Removal Act of 1830, a key policy of President Andrew Jackson. It resulted in the Trail of Tears (1830–1850), in which an estimated 60,000 Native Americans living east of the Mississippi River were forcibly removed and displaced to lands far to the west, causing 13,200 to 16,700 deaths along the forced march.[96] Settler expansion as well as this influx of Indigenous peoples from the East resulted in the American Indian Wars west of the Mississippi.[97][98]

During the colonial period, slavery became legal in all the Thirteen colonies, and by 1770 it provided the main labor force in the large-scale, agriculture-dependent economies of the Southern Colonies from Maryland to Georgia. The practice began to be significantly questioned during the American Revolution,[99] and spurred by an active abolitionist movement that had reemerged in the 1830s, states in the North enacted laws to prohibit slavery within their boundaries.[100] At the same time, support for slavery had strengthened in Southern states, with widespread use of inventions such as the cotton gin (1793) having made slavery immensely profitable for Southern elites.[101][102][103]

The United States annexed the Republic of Texas in 1845,[104] and the 1846 Oregon Treaty led to U.S. control of the present-day American Northwest.[105] Dispute with Mexico over Texas led to the Mexican–American War (1846–1848). After the victory of the U.S., Mexico recognized U.S. sovereignty over Texas, New Mexico, and California in the 1848 Mexican Cession; the cession's lands also included the future states of Nevada, Colorado and Utah.[87][106] The California gold rush of 1848–1849 spurred a huge migration of white settlers to the Pacific coast, leading to even more confrontations with Native populations. One of the most violent, the California genocide of thousands of Native inhabitants, lasted into the mid-1870s.[107] Additional western territories and states were created.[108]

Slave states and free states in 1858

Throughout the 1850s, the sectional conflict regarding slavery was further inflamed by national legislation in the U.S. Congress and decisions of the Supreme Court. In Congress, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 mandated the forcible return to their enslavers in the South of persons taking refuge in non-slave states, while the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 effectively gutted the anti-slavery requirements of the Missouri Compromise.[109] In its Dred Scott decision of 1857, the Supreme Court ruled against an enslaved person brought into non-slave territory, simultaneously declaring the entire Missouri Compromise to be unconstitutional. These and other events exacerbated tensions between North and South that would culminate in the American Civil War (1861–1865).[110][111][112]

Beginning with South Carolina, 11 slave-state governments voted to secede from the United States in 1860–1861, joining to create the Confederate States of America.[113] All other state governments remained loyal to the Union.[s][114][115] War broke out in April 1861 after the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter.[116][117] Following the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, many freed slaves joined the Union army.[118] The war began to turn in the Union's favor following the 1863 Siege of Vicksburg and Battle of Gettysburg, and the Confederates surrendered in 1865 after the Union's victory in the Battle of Appomattox Court House.[119]

Reconstruction, Gilded Age, and Progressive Era (1866–1917)
Main article: History of the United States (1865–1917)
An Edison Studios film showing immigrants arriving at Ellis Island in New York Harbor, a major point of entry for European immigrants in the late 19th and early 20th centuries[120][121]

Efforts toward reconstruction in the secessionist South had begun as early as 1862,[122] but it was only after President Lincoln's assassination that the three Reconstruction Amendments to the Constitution were ratified to protect civil rights. The amendments codified nationally the abolition of slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for crimes, promised equal protection under the law for all persons, and prohibited denial or abridgment of voting rights on the basis of race, color, or previous enslavement.[123][124][125][126] As a result,

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Geographical dictionary or directory used in conjunction with a map or atlas

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Ordnance_Gazetteer_for_Scotland_-_Title_Page.jpg/250px-Ordnance_Gazetteer_for_Scotland_-_Title_Page.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ordnance_Gazetteer_for_Scotland_-_Title_Page.jpg)

Ordnance Gazetteer for Scotland – title page

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Gazetteers-2.jpg/250px-Gazetteers-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gazetteers-2.jpg)

Ordnance Gazetteer for Scotland – first page

In [geography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography "Geography"), a **gazetteer** is a [dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictionary "Dictionary")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-Macmillan-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-Webster's_and_Roget's-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-Webster's_New_Dictionary-3) or [directory](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/directory "wikt:directory") used in conjunction with a map or [atlas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas "Atlas").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-aurousseau_61-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-OED-5) It typically contains information concerning the geographical makeup, [social statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_statistics "Social statistics") and physical features of a country, region, or continent. Content of a gazetteer can include a subject's location, dimensions of peaks and waterways, [population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_population "Statistical population"), [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") and literacy rate. This information is generally divided into topics with entries listed in alphabetical order.

[Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") gazetteers are known to have existed since the [Hellenistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_civilization "Hellenistic civilization") era. The first known Chinese gazetteer was released by the first century, and with the age of print media in [China by the ninth century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_typography_in_East_Asia "History of typography in East Asia"), the [Chinese gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentry_(China) "Gentry (China)") became invested in producing gazetteers for their local areas as a source of information as well as local pride. The geographer [Stephanus of Byzantium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanus_of_Byzantium "Stephanus of Byzantium") wrote a geographical dictionary (which currently has missing parts) in the sixth century which influenced later European compilers. Modern gazetteers can be found in reference sections of most [libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libraries "Libraries") as well as on the internet.

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gazetteer&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The _[Oxford English Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford\_English\_Dictionary "Oxford English Dictionary")_ defines a "gazetteer" as a "geographical index or dictionary".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1968658-6) It includes as an example a work by the British historian [Laurence Echard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Echard "Laurence Echard") (d.1730) in 1693 that bore the title "The Gazetteer's: or Newsman's Interpreter: Being a Geographical Index".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1968658-6) Echard wrote that the title "Gazetteer's" was suggested to him by a "very eminent person" whose name he chose not to disclose.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1968658-6) For Part II of this work published in 1704, Echard referred to the book simply as "the Gazeteer". This marked the introduction of the word "gazetteer" into the [English language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1968658-6) Historian Robert C. White suggests that the "very eminent person" written of by Echard was his colleague [Edmund Bohun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Bohun "Edmund Bohun"), and chose not to mention Bohun because he became associated with the [Jacobite movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobitism "Jacobitism").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1968658-6)

Since the 18th century, the word "gazetteer" has been used interchangeably to define either its traditional meaning (i.e.,a geographical dictionary or directory) or a daily [newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper "Newspaper"), such as the _London Gazetteer_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-thomas_623_636-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazetteer#cite_note-asquith_703_724-8)

## Types and organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gazetteer&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Types and organization")]

Gazetteers are often categorized by the type, and scope, of the information presented. _**World gazetteers**_ usually consist of an alphabetical listing of countries, with pertinent [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics") for each one, with some gazetteers listing information on individual [cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities "Cities"), [towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town "Town"), [villages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villages "Villages"),

Representatives of the Compact states meeting in [Kolonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolonia "Kolonia"), [Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_States_of_Micronesia "Federated States of Micronesia"), in August 2019. Left to right: U.S. secretary of state [Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo"), Micronesian president [David Panuelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Panuelo "David Panuelo"), Marshallese president [Hilda Heine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_Heine "Hilda Heine"), and Palauan vice president [Raynold Oilouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynold_Oilouch "Raynold Oilouch")

The **Compacts of Free Association** (**COFA**) are international agreements establishing and governing the relationships of [free association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_state "Associated state") between the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and the three [Pacific Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania")[sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state"): [Federated States of Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_States_of_Micronesia "Federated States of Micronesia") (FSM), the [Republic of the Marshall Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Islands "Marshall Islands") (RMI), and the [Republic of Palau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palau "Palau"). As a result, these countries are sometimes known as the **Freely Associated States** (**FASs**). All three agreements next expire in 2043.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_of_Free_Association#cite_note-1)

These countries, together with the [Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands"), formerly constituted the [Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_Territory_of_the_Pacific_Islands "Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands"), a [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations")[trusteeship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_trust_territories "United Nations trust territories") administered by the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") from 1947 to 1951, and by the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior") from 1951 to 1986 (to 1994 for Palau).

**North Lima** is an [unincorporated community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unincorporated_area "Unincorporated area") and [census-designated place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census-designated_place "Census-designated place") in [Beaver Township, Mahoning County, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Township,_Mahoning_County,_Ohio "Beaver Township, Mahoning County, Ohio"), United States. The population was 1,369 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-Census_2020-3) Located at the intersection of State Routes [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_Route_7 "Ohio State Route 7"), [164](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_Route_164 "Ohio State Route 164"), and [165](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_Route_165 "Ohio State Route 165"), it is part of the [Youngstown–Warren metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahoning_Valley "Mahoning Valley").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Lima,_Ohio&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

North Lima was [laid out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") around 1826.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-4) The name may be a transfer from [Lima, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima,_New_York "Lima, New York").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-5) A post office called North Lima has been in operation since 1832 which bears the [ZIP code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZIP_code "ZIP code") of 44452.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-7)

The former site of [South Range High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Range_High_School "South Range High School") is located in the town center. The building is now used to host many of the town's local businesses.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-8)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Lima,_Ohio&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Education")]

Children in North Lima are served by the public South Range Local School District, which includes one elementary school, one middle school, and [South Range High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Range_High_School "South Range High School").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio#cite_note-10)

*   [Frank DiLeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_DiLeo "Frank DiLeo"), [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson") manager. Died in a care facility outside Youngstown, Ohio.

It took more than the help of firefighters from eight departments to battle flames at a Beaver Township business on Wednesday.

Putting out a fire that broke out at Bolt Construction along South Avenue also was aided by a couple of local businesses.

The Beaver Township Fire and Rescue Facebook page included appreciation to Sheetz in North Lima for sending apples, oranges, bananas, and water to feed firefighters at the burning warehouse.

Firefighters also sent out a “Thank You” to the North Lima Pizza Joes for quickly preparing pizza for crews fighting the flames.

In addition to Beaver Township, firefighters from New Springfield, Western Reserve Fire District, Cardinal Joint Fire District, Columbiana, New Waterford, Green Township, and Mahoning County Haz-Mat Team all took part in the effort.

NORTH LIMA -- For Kasey McDade, 2020 hasn't been too bad, considering how it began.

"I'm thankful for where I'm at now because of what happened," she said.

On Jan. 15, she escaped a fire at her Boardman apartment wearing the clothes on her back and with her senior dog, Stewie, safe by her side. Everything else was lost.

When the blaze happened at her London Square Apartment on Rockdale Avenue in Boardman, McDade, 28, was waiting to hear from a possible job lead.

On Jan. 16, her phone rang.

"When I saw the phone ringing, I thought, 'This is it. There's a reason this happened.'"

The phone call was to tell McDade that she did not get the job. But shortly after is when her luck began to turn around.

She received a call from her current employer, the Blood and Cancer Center in Canfield, asking her to come in for an interview.

Initially, she said she was a little hesitant because the medical assistant position was part time, but she figured it was a great opportunity.

Just two weeks later, it became a full-time position that she loves and is thankful for.

"I just love my job so much," she said.

That new job has helped McDade get a new car and start saving for a house, "which wasn't always on the horizon," she said.

In a bittersweet turn of events, Stewie is unable to live with her at her mother's house in North Lima. He can't manage the steps.

Still, she's thankful he has a good life in a good home.

McDade said her mother, Evangela, has been a pillar of support since the fire.

They've always been close, but living together has allowed their bond to grow, McDade said. "She's my rock."

Also showing support to McDade through the year has been the community, stepping up to donate clothes and home items after the fire.

"It still leaves me speechless when I think about it," she said.

When she runs errands around town, she sees familiar faces now, because of their generosity while she's been rebuilding. That sense of community support resonated with McDade.

She tries to do more random acts of kindness for others, whether it's participating in activities for senior citizens or buying a snack for a coworker.

Perhaps the happiest news is she may be hearing wedding bells in the future, as she and an old friend reconnected this year, eventually deciding to start a relationship.

McDade said this year, she's learned that people should expect the unexpected, but keep moving forward.

"In general, whatever path you think you're on, you're not. You have to have faith in yourself," she said.

To remind herself to keep that faith, she got the word tattoed on her forearm.

"You are stronger than you think you are. You just don't know until you're put to the test," she said.

For 2021, McDade wants to keep the momentum she's gained this year. "My plan is honestly to just take one day at a time and enjoy each and every day, even the rough days."

McDade said that although 2020 started on a bad note, she's going to be careful what she wishes for in the new year, because as she learned this year, anything can happen.

"If you want chocolate ice cream, you have to ask specifically for chocolate ice cream. Otherwise you're going to end up with chocolate ice cream, walnuts and pecans, and whatever else in it."

MINERAL RIDGE -- A special display is inside the Moss Ancestral Home showcasing the ancestors of local residents who served in the Revolutionary War as part of America's 250th celebration this year.

Marcy Buchanan, president of the Mineral Ridge Historical Society, said Mary Lou Godleski, curator of the Moss House, has done research on the histories of Mineral Ridge and Weathersfield residents. including the Buchanan family and family of historical society member Linda Ference.

"She has compiled the history and ancestors of many Mineral Ridge residents who live here or have ties to Mineral Ridge. Mary Lou has researched the families to see if they have any ancestors who served in the Revolutionary War,'' Buchanan said.

A display of the history of the local families is on the wall inside the house.

More than 30 families from the area are showcased on the wall. highlighting the members who served during the Revolutionary War.

Godleski, who recently celebrated her 90th birthday, said she is active with the Daughters of the American Revolution and wanted to gather information on William Dunlap who was a Revolutionary War soldier who built the Moss House.

She also made a small booklet of the names of Revolutionary War soldiers who helped from the area.

Buchanan said this year the Mineral Ridge Historical Society has been focused on programs and displays related to America's 250th.

Godleski said she used different ancestry sites as MyHeritage, Ancestry and familysearch.org and was able to locate many patriots connected with local families.

"Some of the local families did not come here until after the 1800s so they may or may not have had any relatives who served in the Revolutionary War,;'' she said.

Brandon Fisher, a historical society member, said he was impressed when Godleski found some of his relatives from the Revolutionary War period.

"Mary Lou wants people to remember their ancestors who served and protected our country,'' he said.

Buchanan said the display will stay on the wall through the year for the monthly open houses held the second Sunday of each month through November.

Bill Moss, who for many years has done programs at the Moss House on Native Americans, said Godleski is a relative who has put in a lot of time doing research on local families.

Buchanan said Samuel Holden Parsons, who was a general in the Revolutionary War, purchased the salt springs in the township in 1788.

Godleski said after finding information on William Dunlap and his connection with the Moss House she knew she wanted to do more and find out the names of others who are connected to the township and the Revolutionary War.

She said she hopes people enjoy the display as well as the many other items displayed inside the house.

Keith McComb of Mineral Ridge said his ancestors were interesting to learn about and how they contributed to the community,

"It is fascinating to see the many local residents who did much for the community,'' he said.

McComb said he was fascinated by the history of the Dunlap family and their contribution to the Moss House.

## North Lima, OH Map

North Lima, Ohio is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) situated in eastern Beaver Township, Mahoning County. As of the 2025 US Census, the population of North Lima is approximately 1,314 residents. The community is located at the intersection of State Routes 7, 164, and 165 and is part of the Youngstown–Warren metropolitan area. Historically, North Lima was laid out in 1826, with a post office established in 1832, and it is believed that the town's name was derived from Lima, New York.

The local landscape features a mix of residential and rural-suburban characteristics. One notable landmark is the former South Range High School, which has been repurposed to accommodate various local businesses. For outdoor activities, nearby parks and recreational areas provide green spaces for residents. The small community atmosphere fosters a close-knit environment, contributing to its identity as a quiet residential area.

In terms of entertainment and family-friendly options, North Lima hosts several local events and gatherings, reflecting its communal spirit. While nightlife and extensive entertainment venues may be limited, the proximity to the larger Youngstown area offers additional options for dining and entertainment. The community's historical roots and ongoing local development continue to shape its character and appeal.

Nearby cities include: [Boardman Twp](link_28), [New Springfield](link_29), [Columbiana](link_30), [Poland](link_31), [New Middletown](link_32), [Petersburg](link_33), [Washingtonville](link_34), [Canfield](link_35), [Leetonia](link_36), [Struthers](link_37).

# [Mental Health Counseling Services](link_17) at Meridian HealthCare close to North Lima

You don’t have to struggle through mood swings and depression on your own. With help from Meridian HealthCare, you can learn to handle common daily life stressors and recognize the warning signs and symptoms of depression.

Our counselors and mental health professionals provide patient-centered, individual counseling, and come up with a treatment plan inclusive of a level of care that is specific to the problems you’re facing. They are trained in an evidence-based therapy that can positively impact many types of mental illnesses and a variety of concerns:

*   Mood Disorders
*   Adjustment Difficulties
*   Anxiety Disorders (Panic Disorders)
*   Depression
*   Phases of Life Issues
*   Divorce
*   Grief
*   Birth of a Child
*   Adoption
*   Trauma
*   OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder)
*   PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder)
*   Phobias

_*If you are experiencing a health crisis, call 911._

![Image 20: Counseling-circle](https://meridianhealthcare.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Counseling-circle.jpg)

## Finding a Trusted Therapist near North Lima, Ohio…

Treatment options are different for everyone. Meridian’s health providers deliver the best in psychotherapy, also commonly referred to as talk therapy, giving you insight and knowledge to cope and better manage stress (without the side effects of mood stabilizers or anti-anxiety medications). Our experienced mental health specialists have your well-being in mind and work with you so that you feel comfortable and confident at every session.

No physician referral is needed to utilize the mental health center services through Meridian – individuals can be self-referred or referred by family members, friends, community organizations or other Meridian programs.

### Does Insurance Cover Counseling Costs?

Meridian HealthCare accepts Medicaid, private insurance, and self-pay (which is based on a sliding scale according to your income) for mental health counseling services. There is also a limited amount of funds available for patients without a payer source, based on their location.

## Adolescent/Teen Mental Health Counseling in North Lima, Ohio

Mental health counseling may be beneficial for teens dealing with the issues that are common for young people today. Mental health care not only helps to address many medical conditions, but it’s also a great avenue for adolescents who just need to talk and be heard. Concerns are addressed on a one-to-one basis with our trained mental health counselors/licensed therapists.

Adolescent mental health counseling is beneficial in a variety of circumstances:

*   Depression
*   Bullying
*   School Problems
*   Trauma
*   Family Problems
*   Grief
*   Low Self-Esteem

*   Impulsive Behaviors
*   General behavioral Problems
*   Generalized Anxiety Disorder
*   Gambling
*   Suicidal Thoughts
*   Eating Disorders

## Mental Health and How It Relates to Substance Abuse

Addressing mental health conditions sometimes involves confronting substance use disorders, as well. Meridian’s treatment programs are designed to address the entire individual with support services to ensure total wellness.

We are proud to provide individual counseling and care services to anyone who needs assistance in coping with a life stressor. Our substance abuse treatment options and recovery programs are designed to be unique for each individual, no matter their age or circumstance.

True health means having hope for a better tomorrow, and the counselors/staff at Meridian are ready to help you find your path to wellness.

## Call [Meridian HealthCare](link_0)’s Behavioral Health Services Today!

Whether you’re seeking one-on-one counseling, family therapy, group discussions or telehealth services, Meridian HealthCare is here for you! We are proud to be the area’s premier integrated health system for behavioral health services, primary care, chiropractic treatment, acupuncture and addiction recovery services.

Accredited by the Joint Commission, one of the most respected names in healthcare, Meridian works to continuously evolve as the concept of integrative care becomes the benchmark for healthcare providers worldwide.

Whether you’re searching for a primary care doctor, dual diagnosis management, medication-free pain relief, or a listening ear for yourself or a loved one, Meridian HealthCare is here! The power of care is nothing without hope. And every service we offer is created with true healing in mind. Find YOUR hope at Meridian.

## About Ohio

[Ohio](link_35) is a state in the [Midwestern region](link_36) of the United States. Of the fifty states, it is the 34th-largest by area, and with a population of nearly 11.8 million, is the seventh-most populous and tenth-most densely populated.

Things To Do in Ohio:

[Cuyahoga Valley National Park](link_37)

## About North Lima, Ohio

[North Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lima,_Ohio) is an [unincorporated community](link_40) and census-designated place in central Beaver Township, Mahoning County, Ohio, United States.

Population: 3,515 (2019)

Area code: 330

[Mill Creek Preserve](link_42)

### What county is North Lima in?

Mahoning County

### How did North Lima Ohio gets its name?

The name may be a transfer from Lima, New York. A post office called North Lima has been in operation since 1832 which bears the ZIP code of 44452. The former site of South Range High School is located in the town center. The building is now used to host many of the town’s local businesses.

44452

# Shop Boardman.

We're excited to introduce the first step toward a future vision for Boardman Park- offering unique park merchandise and local products that celebrate our community.

Our brand-new **Boardman Park blankets** are now available for purchase through the Park Office! They're perfect for Music in the Park, Boardman Community Day, summer movie nights, picnics, and finding a comfortable spot to enjoy this year's fireworks celebration honoring America's 250th anniversary.

Boardman Park welcomes thousands of visitors each year. Whether you're taking a lunch break, hanging out at the playground, attending an event, or simply enjoying a moment in nature, these blankets are a great way to show your park pride.

Every purchase gives back! Proceeds help support recreation programs, educational opportunities, park beautification projects, historical preservation, natural resource stewardship, and community events that make Boardman Park special.

Blankets are available through the Park Office. Please call ahead to reserve yours or arrange pickup while supplies last.

This is just the beginning, and we're excited to continue exploring new ways to connect local products, community pride, and support for the park in the future.

## North Lima, OH Map

North Lima, Ohio is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) situated in eastern Beaver Township, Mahoning County. As of the 2025 US Census, the population of North Lima is approximately 1,314 residents. The community is located at the intersection of State Routes 7, 164, and 165 and is part of the Youngstown–Warren metropolitan area. Historically, North Lima was laid out in 1826, with a post office established in 1832, and it is believed that the town's name was derived from Lima, New York.

The local landscape features a mix of residential and rural-suburban characteristics. One notable landmark is the former South Range High School, which has been repurposed to accommodate various local businesses. For outdoor activities, nearby parks and recreational areas provide green spaces for residents. The small community atmosphere fosters a close-knit environment, contributing to its identity as a quiet residential area.

In terms of entertainment and family-friendly options, North Lima hosts several local events and gatherings, reflecting its communal spirit. While nightlife and extensive entertainment venues may be limited, the proximity to the larger Youngstown area offers additional options for dining and entertainment. The community's historical roots and ongoing local development continue to shape its character and appeal.

NORTH LIMA – One person is dead from a single-vehicle crash that happened at about 10:30 a.m. today on state Route 626 near state Route 164.

According to the Ohio State Highway Patrol, the vehicle traveled off of the right side of the road, struck a culvert and came to rest in a ditch. The vehicle caught fire and was extinguished by Beaver Township Fire Department. The driver was deceased when safety personnel arrived.

The name of the person, who was not wearing a seatbelt, is being withheld pending notification of relatives. The state patrol is investigating.

## Jonathan David Panick Obituary

Jonathan David Panick, 32   
  
  
  
 North Lima - Jonathan David Panick, 32, passed away tragically from an automobile accident Tuesday morning, April 13, 2021.   
  
  
  
 Jonathan, known by his family and friends as "Jon," was born October 8, 1988 in Youngstown, the son of Linda M. Berry and William C. Panick, Sr.   
  
  
  
 He graduated from Cardinal Mooney High School in 2007. Jon later attended St. Bonaventure University in New York and Columbus Community College in Ohio, studying construction management.   
  
  
  
 He worked in commercial construction throughout the country.   
  
  
  
 During his earlier years, Jon played recreational soccer and baseball. When attending Cardinal Mooney High School, he played football. He enjoyed snow skiing, golf, camping, and being in the great outdoors.   
  
  
  
 Jon was a devoted son and brother. He loved spending time with his family.   
  
  
  
 Jon is survived by his mother, Linda M. Berry of North Lima; his father, William C. Panick, Sr of Boardman; two brothers, James R. Best of Youngstown and William C. Panick, Jr. of Struthers; his uncles, Bruce (Pat) Berry of Poland, Dennis Berry of Struthers, Thomas Berry of Boardman, Rick (MaryJo) Berry of North Lima, James Berry of Poland, and Ed Berry of Lake Milton; three aunts, Janet Ruehle of Poland, MaryLou (Chuck) Korda of Boardman, and Julie (Gary) Heasley of Chester Springs, PA; many close cousins; and his girlfriend, Marissa Wong of San Francisco, CA.   
  
  
  
 Jon was preceded in death by his grandparents, Robert and Mary Berry, Charles and Dorothy Panick and his Uncle, David Ruehle.   
  
  
  
 Family and friends may call on Monday, April 19, 2021, from 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. and on Tuesday, April 20, 2021, from 10:00 to 10:45 a.m. at Davis-Becker Funeral Home, 8536 Market Street in Boardman. There will be a funeral service celebrating Jon's life on Tuesday at 11:00 a.m. at the funeral home with Pastor MaryJo Berry officiating. Interment will follow at St. John the Baptist Cemetery. Due to COVID-19, the 6-foot rule will be honored, and we politely ask that all guests, whose health allows, wear a mask.   
  
  
  
 Condolences may be sent at www.beckerobits.com.

SKATEPARK EVENT: The Youngstown Skate Park Association and Parks and Recreation Department will have a pop-up skate park 1 to 4 p.m. Saturday at Glenwood Community Park, 2538 Glenwood Avenue in Youngstown. The free community-focused event will temporarily transform a portion of the city parks property into a skatepark and provide an opportunity for action sports opportunities for neighborhoods throughout Youngstown. Helmets are mandatory for those under age 18.

HISTORICAL SOCIETY LECTURE: The Springfield Township Historical Society Museum continues its "Afternoon at the Museum: speaker series at 2 p.m. Sunday at the museum, 14188 Youngstown Pittsburgh Road in Petersburg. Frank DeRhodes will talk about the 80-year history of the New Middletown Farmers and Sportsman Club. He will talk about the club's contributions to conservation and the education of youth to hunting and fishing. The program is free. The museum opens at 1:30 p.m.

COOK OFF: The Annual Guly’s Cook Off will be 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturday at the Hungarian Cultural Center of Northeastern Ohio in Hiram. The cost is $10 per adult and includes a ballot to vote. Children under 12 years are free. A fun-filled afternoon sampling many tastes of Guly'as. There will be People's Choice winners and Judge Choice winners. Hot dogs, bakery and beverages are also available for purchase.

To register, call Linda Mantz at 440-248-4530 or Lorand Csibi at 440-360-0595.

HAZARDOUS WASTE COLLECTION: A household hazardous waste collection will be from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday at the Canfield Fairgrounds on state Route 46, Gate 9. For Mahoning County households only. No businesses.

Various items will be accepted. Items not accepted are explosives, pharmaceuticals and latex paint. There will be a five-gallon limit on all containers. Collection and drop-off items will be based on last name. A-G will be from 9 to 11 a.m G-N from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. and O-Z from 1 to 3 p.m. For information call 330-740-2060.

FOOD FEST: Archangel Michael Greek Orthodox Church, 401 12th Street in Campbell will have a Greek food fest from noon to 10 p.m. today and Saturday and noon to 8 p.m. Sunday. Admission is free. There will be a variety of Greek food and pastries games for children and cultural and religious items for sale. For information call 330-755-9072.

TRASH AND TREASURE SALE: Grace Lutheran Church, 162 South Raccoon Road, is having a trash and treasure sale starting at 9 am. Saturday. This is an all-day, one-day sale. Items include clothes, housewares, tools and antiques. The men’s and women’s groups of the church work together to have the sale. The funds are used for major repair and improvement projects.

ONEOHIO MEETING: The OneOhio Region 7 Collaborative of the OneOhio Foundation will meet at 5 p.m. on Monday at Direction Home of Eastern Ohio, 1030 North Meridian Road.

COIN CLUB MEETING: The Wheatland Mercer County Coin Club will hold its monthly meeting Wednesday at the Wheatland American Legion, 2 Cherry Street, Wheatland, Pa.

This month members will plan a special raffle, main raffle, coin auction, birthday prizes and more. Every member will be awarded one free coin and may participate in the raffles. Light refreshments are available.

Members are encouraged to act as vendors and may sell coins before the meeting.

AUSTINTOWN -- The Canfield Post of the Ohio State Highway Patrol is investigating a two-vehicle fatal crash that occurred at approximately 03:07 a.m. Thursday, according to an OHP press release.

At approximately 03:07 a.m., a 2026 Freightliner Cascadia semi, driven by Justin Hinds, 55, of Conyers, Georgia, was traveling westbound on Interstate 80 near mile post 222. At that time a 2010 Ford Crown Victoria, driven by Theodore Sisak, 35, of Erie, Pennsylvania, quickly approached the semi from the rear. Sisak's vehicle struck the trailer causing fatal injuries to himself, according to the release.

Assisting on scene were the Austintown Police Department, Austintown Fire and EMS, Mahoning County coroner, and Lane LifeTrans.

Speed appears to be a factor in this crash. The crash remains under investigation.

# Former Ohio missionary pleads guilty to molesting 2 boys in Haiti

September 9, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.vindy.com?ID=398740&category=4)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Former%20Ohio%20missionary%20pleads%20guilty%20to%20molesting%202%20boys%20in%20Haiti&url=https://www.vindy.com?ID=398740&category=4)

![Image 2: Missionary Abuse Haiti](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.oniwire.com/images/2026/09/09014058/AP26251742946308-470x300.jpg%20480w)Lake Fong/Pittsburgh Post-Gazett

Jeriah Mast, a former missionary for Christian Aid Ministries, is taken into custody after his sentencing at Holmes County Courthouse Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2019 in Millersburg, Ohio. (Lake Fong/Pittsburgh Post-Gazette via AP)

## Trending

[1 ##### Reported accident has Mooney athlete on life support](https://www.vindy.com/sports/2026/09/reported-accident-has-mooney-athlete-on-life-support/)[2 ##### Oct. 3-4 Property transfers](https://www.vindy.com/news/2026/10/oct-3-4-property-transfers/)[3 ##### NFL suspends York, fines him $500,000 after trafficking arrest](https://www.vindy.com/news/local-news/2026/10/nfl-suspends-york-fines-him-500000-after-trafficking-arrest/)[4 ##### Canfield officials give updates at chamber event](https://www.vindy.com/news/2026/10/canfield-officials-give-updates-at-chamber-event/)[5 ##### Girard outlasts South Range in high-scoring meeting](https://www.vindy.com/sports/2026/10/girard-outlasts-south-range-in-high-scoring-meeting/)[6 ##### Youngstown man acquitted in teen’s death](https://www.vindy.com/news/2026/10/youngstown-man-acquitted-in-teens-death/)[7 ##### Mooney’s Durst taken off life support](https://www.vindy.com/sports/2026/10/mooneys-durst-taken-off-life-support/)

[view more](https://www.vindy.com/trending/)

 A former missionary with an Ohio-based ministry pleaded guilty Tuesday to federal charges that he sexually abused two boys in Haiti, reaching an agreement with prosecutors that could lead to a prison sentence of at least 25 years.Jeriah Mast, 45, of Millersburg, Ohio -- who told police in 2019 he had molested more than 30 boys in Haiti and four children in Ohio -- entered the plea before Judge Donald C. Nugent in federal court in Cleveland.Under the plea agreement, Mast and prosecutors agreed that an "appropriate" sentence would be between 25 and 33 years, though the judge would have final say. Sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 15.Mast took trips to Haiti for mission work between 2002 and 2019. That included several years of work for the Millersburg-based Christian Aid Ministries, which coordinates missionary activities supported by Amish, conservative Mennonite and related church groups. Mast belonged to a church in a related Anabaptist movement.Mast's case has drawn attention to wider sexual abuse issues in the conservative, plain-dressing Anabaptist communities, which include Old Order Amish and Mennonites. Advocates have said that amid the movement's strong emphasis on forgiveness, victims have been pressured to reconcile with abusers and not to seek prosecution outside the disciplines of the largely closed religious communities.Mast was arrested on federal charges last November, shortly after he received early release for a sexual abuse conviction in Ohio state court. Mast was formally indicted in December on four federal charges of engaging in illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place.The indictment alleged he abused four boys in Haiti -- one each in 2004 and 2007 and two in 2011.Mast's guilty plea was to charges involving the 2004 case and one of the 2011 cases, each involving a minor between 12 and 16 years old. Prosecutors agreed to move for dismissal of the remaining two charges, according to the plea agreement. But Mast admitted to the factual basis of the remaining charges in the plea agreement.The charges were based on a U.S. law that prohibits citizens from engaging "in any illicit sexual conduct with another person" overseas, according to court filings.Mast's attorney filed a motion in May to get the charges dismissed, saying the law exceeded the constitutionality of Congress' ability to regulate citizens' conduct overseas. The court denied the motion in August. The plea agreement indicates Mast reserved the right to appeal that ruling."This type of predatory conduct -- committed by someone entrusted with missionary work -- represents a profound betrayal of trust, and today's plea is an important step toward justice for the many victims harmed by Mast's actions," said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the U.S. Department of Justice's Criminal Division, in a statement.Mast's attorney did not return a phone message left Tuesday with his office.Tuesday marked the second time Mast pleaded guilty in a sexual-abuse case. He was sentenced in Holmes County court in 2019 to nine years in prison on state charges of gross sexual imposition involving two boys in Ohio.But in October 2025, Mast received an early judicial release from state prison and was placed on probation.Retired Judge Edward Emmett O'Farrell of neighboring Tuscarawas County granted his release based on "an exemplary record" behind bars and "most importantly, the Defendant's stated and demonstrated remorse for the crimes he committed, and the emotional and psychological pain and suffering he inflicted upon the child victims and their families in this case."U.S. authorities had previously been investigating Mast's actions in Haiti, but the probe had remained largely dormant while Mast was in state prison.Federal prosecutors "accelerated" their investigation after learning of Mast's early release from state prison, according to federal court records.Holmes County, where Christian Aid Ministries is based, is the hub of one of the nation's largest Amish settlements and also has significant Mennonite and related church populations.In 2019, CAM placed two of its managers on leave amid revelations that they knew as early as 2013 that Mast had confessed to sexual misconduct, yet kept him on the job.CAM's work in Haiti came into the international spotlight in 2021 when 17 missionaries and their children were kidnapped by a gang. They went free later that year, some ransomed by a third party, CAM acknowledged. CAM said most of the rest escaped. ___ AP photographer Sue Ogrocki contributed. ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP's collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. HENDERSON, Nev. -- William A. "Bill" Proverbs passed away peacefully in his sleep on Aug. 24, 2026, at the age of 94, at his home in Henderson, Nevada.

Bill was born on Sept. 19, 1931, in Youngstown, Ohio, a son of the late William and Cora Graham Proverbs. He was preceded in death by his brother, James M. Proverbs, and sister, Shirley Welsh Lewis.

He leaves behind his beloved wife of 51 years, Patricia Scott Proverbs. He also leaves sisters-in-law, Phyllis (Paul) Schneider and Marjorie Theophilus; 11 nieces and nephews; and 10 great-grandnieces and great-grandnephews, who will forever cherish memories of their Uncle Bill.

One of his many passions throughout his life was baseball. He pitched in the Cleveland Indians organization from 1950 to 1956. After an arm injury brought his baseball career to an early end, Bill proudly served in the United States Army.

Upon returning to civilian life, Bill continued his education at Hiram College, earning his bachelor's degree in health and physical education in 1958. He received his master's degree in education in 1962 from Kent State University. Bill remained at Hiram College as head coach of the baseball and volleyball programs and as an assistant coach in football and basketball. After 31 years he retired.

Bill's dedication to athletics and education earned him many honors throughout his life. Among his proudest achievements were his inductions into the Chaney High School Hall of Fame, the Hiram College Hall of Fame and the Curbstone Coaches Hall of Fame. Another honor was the renaming of Robert O. Fishel Field to Fishel Field at Proverbs Park in Hiram.

His influence extended beyond the playing field, and the relationships he built with his players were a source of great pride and joy. Many remained in contact with him throughout their adult lives.

Outside of baseball and coaching, Bill enjoyed playing golf and painting. His oil paintings became cherished gifts to family and friends, with many proudly displayed on their walls as lasting reminders of his creativity and generosity.

William was truly blessed throughout his 94 years. He lived a life filled with family, friendship, baseball, coaching, creativity and countless memories. He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing him.

Bill's family would like to thank ProCare Hospice of Nevada for their loving care during Bill's illness.

Interment will take place at a later date at Lake Park Cemetery in Youngstown.

MESA, Ariz. -- Jane M. Kanik, 69, died peacefully on Monday, June 29, 2026, in Mesa, Arizona.

Jane was born on May 9, 1957, in Charleston, W.Va., and grew up in Austintown, Ohio.

Jane graduated from Austintown Fitch High School in 1975 and then earned an associate degree in business from Youngstown State University. She moved to Mesa, Arizona, to join her sisters and their families in 2008.

Jane was known for her smile, kindness and dedication to family. Jane loved to read and volunteered at the library. She enjoyed many of the activities in her community. She was a beloved daughter, sister, aunt and great-aunt.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Florence and Joseph Kanik; and is survived by her sisters, Susan (Dave) Davis and Joan Aeppli; nieces, Allison (Carl) Bandura and Britney (David) Schleif; and nephew, Joe (Brittani) Aeppli; as well as her cherished great-nieces and nephews, Lucy Bandura, Quinn Bandura, Jack Schleif, Emery Schleif, Reagan Aeppli and Banks Aeppli.

She will be greatly missed.

A memorial prayer service will take place at 11 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in the chapel at Resurrection Cemetery in Austintown.

### Obituaries  
& Tributes

Losing someone you love is never easy. At Becker Funeral Homes, we offer a convenient way to find recent services, leave condolences, and share cherished memories online. This resource allows family and friends across Ohio and beyond to honor a life well-lived and connect in remembrance.

### Funeral and Cremation Services near Boardman OH

Every family is unique, and every tribute should reflect that. Becker Funeral Homes provides funeral and cremation services tailored to your wishes, family traditions, and budget. From time-honored ceremonies to personalized memorials, our team guides you through every step with care, respect, and dignity.

## About Us

Becker Funeral Homes is a proud part of the Mahoning Valley’s history. Founded in 1896 as Cunningham-Davidson Funeral Home in Lowellville, Ohio, our business has served generations of families across multiple communities. Over the decades, the home has expanded into multiple facilities, including our modern Boardman location, while continuing our tradition of warm, personalized service.   
  
Our facilities combine historic elegance with modern comforts, offering welcoming spaces for families to gather, grieve, and celebrate life. Generations of families trust us because we treat each family as our own.

### Memorial  
Services

[Our Memorial Services](https://www.beckerfuneralhomes.com/services/memorial-services)

### Traditional & Burial Services

A traditional funeral service gives family and friends the opportunity to gather, grieve, and honor a life well-lived. At our Mahoning Valley locations, burial services are guided by your family’s wishes and traditions. From visitations and chapel services to graveside gatherings, we help you create a meaningful experience that celebrates your loved one’s life while offering support to those left behind.

### Cremation Services

Many families choose cremation for its simplicity and flexibility. Cremation still allows for a full range of services, including visitations, memorial services, and celebrations of life. Whether you prefer a service before or after cremation, or a gathering at a meaningful location, our staff helps design a tribute that reflects your loved one’s values and legacy.   
  
We also provide guidance on permanent memorialization, including burial of cremated remains, scattering options, or placement in a columbarium or memorial garden.

### Memorial Services – Celebrations of Life

Memorial services allow family and friends to gather without a casket present. These services may be held days, weeks, or even months after a passing, giving loved ones the time and space to plan a service that reflects the life being honored.   
  
Our funeral homes help families throughout Boardman, Struthers, Poland, and surrounding communities plan memorials that are deeply personal—whether in our facilities, a church, a community center, or a meaningful outdoor space.

### Ash Scattering  
Services

For families choosing cremation, we provide resources and guidance on how and where to [scatter ashes](https://www.beckerfuneralhomes.com/services/ash-scattering-services) respectfully. Whether at a meaningful local site, family property, or a designated scattering garden, we help make this farewell personal and heartfelt.

### Veterans Services

We are proud to honor those who have served our country. Becker Funeral Homes offers [veterans services](https://www.beckerfuneralhomes.com/services/veterans-services) that include assistance with military honors, burial in national cemeteries, and presentation of the American flag to family members. We consider it a sacred duty to ensure every veteran is recognized with dignity and respect.
